15.title: the call to prayer, and why it's beautiful even if you don't know the words
15.hook: the call to prayer, and why it's beautiful even if you don't know the words
15.howItsDone: In Muslim-majority places a mu'adhdhin gives the adhan from the mosque, often by loudspeaker, at each of the five prayer times; elsewhere many Muslims hear it from an app, and many families whisper it into a newborn's ear.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salat, the prayer in its set shape, five times a day. Your line was the body prays too. Did you change your posture at a hard moment? Day fifteen.

Maybe you've heard it on a trip, or in a film, or from an app on a friend's phone. A single voice, rising, holding a note much longer than seems possible, then falling away. People who don't understand a word of Arabic stop walking to listen. Travelers write about the first time they heard it at dawn in Istanbul or Cairo, the call rolling across the rooftops from a hundred minarets, never quite in sync. It isn't music, exactly. It's an invitation, five times a day, in the same words for fourteen centuries. Today: the call, and what it's actually saying.
screen: `ONE VOICE, HOLDING A NOTE.` → `A HUNDRED MINARETS AT DAWN.` → `WHAT IS IT SAYING?`

segments.voice: The adhan. The root, a-dh-n, is the root of the ear, udhun. The call is literally the thing you hear. In the first years in Medina, the hadith collections say, the young community didn't have one. People gathered by guessing the time. The companions talked it over: a bell, like the Christians? A horn, like the Jews? A fire? Then, in a report in Abu Dawud, a companion named Abdullah ibn Zayd dreamed of a man teaching him the words. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said it was a true dream, and told him: teach it to Bilal, his voice carries. Bilal ibn Rabah had been enslaved in Mecca and tortured for his faith: he is the man you met on day ten, saying ahad, one, under the rock. Then he was freed. He became the first voice of the call. Now, the words. Allahu akbar: God is greater. Four times. Then two witnesses: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. Then the heart of it. Hayya 'ala s-salah: come to prayer. Hayya 'ala l-falah: come to success. Falah is flourishing, and its root is the root of the farmer, the one who splits the ground so something can grow. At dawn, Sunni callers add a line: prayer is better than sleep. Shia callers add: come to the best of deeds. And many Muslim families whisper the adhan into a newborn's ear, so the first words a child hears are a call. That's why it's beautiful even without the Arabic. Its whole job is to turn toward you and say: come. You, specifically. Now.
screen: `ADHAN — FROM THE ROOT FOR EAR.` · `A DREAM, AND BILAL'S VOICE.` · `COME TO PRAYER. COME TO SUCCESS.` · `WHISPERED TO A NEWBORN.` · then, large: `HAYYA 'ALA L-FALAH.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Close your eyes and listen. Not to anything in particular. Just to what's calling right now. A car outside, the fridge, your own breathing, someone's voice in another room. Each one is asking for a little of your attention. Notice what you turn toward. If you pray, you can let the old words sit under the sound: come to prayer, come to success. The bell holds the time.
The adhan. The call to prayer, from the root for ear. God is greater; come to prayer; come to success. Fifteenth word.
Your line: you are being called. Today, when your phone buzzes or someone says your name, pause for one breath before you answer, and ask what's really calling you. Day fifteen.

16.title: friday
16.hook: Friday; why the week has a hinge
16.howItsDone: On Fridays, many Muslims bathe, dress well and go to the mosque at midday for the khutbah and a two-unit congregational prayer that replaces the noon prayer, then return to work or school.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the adhan, the call to prayer. Come to prayer, come to success. Your line was you are being called. What called you yesterday? Day sixteen.

It's just after noon on a Friday, in a city anywhere. A cab driver parks and locks the car. A nurse swaps her shift. A teenager slips out of the office in a borrowed tie. A shopkeeper pulls the shutter halfway down. They're all walking the same way, and the sidewalk outside the mosque fills until people are praying on mats laid out on the street. Forty minutes later, they're all walking back, and the city takes up exactly where it left off. It's a small weekly miracle of logistics. Today: the day the Muslim week turns on.
screen: `FRIDAY, JUST AFTER NOON.` → `EVERYONE WALKING ONE WAY.` → `THEN BACK TO WORK.`

segments.voice: Jumu'ah. The name for Friday comes from the root j-m-', to gather. The same root gives jami', the big gathering mosque, and jama'ah, the congregation. Friday is, literally, gathering day. The Qur'an sets it up in a surah named after it. In Pickthall's words: “When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading.” Leave your trading. Stop the sale, close the laptop. But listen to the next verse: “And when the prayer is ended, then disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty.” Go back to work. So Friday isn't a day of rest the way some calendars have one. It's a hinge. The week swings on it for an hour, then carries on. What happens in that hour? A sermon, the khutbah, given in two parts, and then a prayer of two units that takes the place of the usual noon prayer. The hadith collections add the preparation: wash the whole body, wear your best clothes, put on perfume, come early. A hadith in Muslim's collection calls Friday the best day the sun rises on: the day Adam was created, and the day he entered the garden. Another, in Bukhari, says there's an hour on Friday when any prayer asked of God is answered, and nobody knows exactly which hour. Most Sunni scholars hold Friday prayer required for men and welcome for women. Shia jurists have differed over when it's required, and many Shia communities hold it every week. The point is in the name: once a week, you show up, together.
screen: `JUMU'AH — FROM A ROOT FOR GATHERING.` · `LEAVE YOUR TRADING.` · `THEN GO BACK TO WORK.` · `THE BEST DAY THE SUN RISES ON.` · then, large: `HASTE UNTO REMEMBRANCE OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Think of the people you actually gather with. A family table, a team, a group chat, a few friends at the same café. Picture their faces, one at a time. Notice who you haven't gathered with in a long while. Let one name come up and stay. If you pray, you can remember them in it. If you don't, just hold their face a little longer. The bell holds the time.
Jumu'ah. Friday, gathering day: a sermon and a prayer at noon, then back to work. The hinge of the week. Sixteenth word.
Your line: gather. Before this week ends, get together with that person whose name came up. A coffee, a call, a meal. Show up. Day sixteen.

17.title: remembrance
17.hook: remembrance; a word repeated on the fingers, and the still watching (muraqaba) that sits beside it
17.tomorrow: a month of not-eating that's really a month of paying attention
17.howItsDone: Many Muslims say short phrases of dhikr after each prayer and through the day, counting on their fingers or on prayer beads. In many Sufi orders, dhikr is also chanted together, and muraqaba is a sitting practice of stillness, watching the heart and breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jumu'ah, Friday, gathering day. Your line was gather. Did you reach out to the person whose name came up? Day seventeen.

Watch someone's hands on a bus in Cairo, or Karachi, or Birmingham, Alabama. Sometimes the thumb is moving across the fingers, joint by joint, very lightly, while their lips move without sound. Or a string of beads is sliding through their fingers, one bead at a time, while they wait for their stop. They aren't counting money or steps. They're doing the thing the whole of Islam keeps circling back to. You met a piece of it on day three, alhamdulillah said after the prayer. Today, the practice behind it, and its quieter sister: saying nothing at all, and watching.
screen: `A THUMB ACROSS THE FINGERS.` → `BEADS ON THE BUS.` → `REMEMBRANCE, AND ITS QUIET SISTER.`

segments.voice: Dhikr. The root, dh-k-r, means to remember, and also to mention, to say aloud. In Arabic those are almost the same act: to remember someone is to bring their name up. The Qur'an even calls itself adh-dhikr, the reminder. And it makes a promise with this word. In Pickthall's words: “Therefore remember Me, I will remember you.” You remember, and you're remembered back. What does it sound like? Short phrases, said again and again. Subhan Allah: glory be to God. Alhamdulillah. Allahu akbar: God is greater. Hadith reports in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi describe the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ counting his dhikr on the fingers of his right hand, and telling people the fingers too will be asked, and will speak. Many Muslims use prayer beads, a misbaha; some scholars prefer the fingers, many are content with either. Now the quiet sister. In Islam's mystical tradition, Sufism, there's a practice called muraqaba, watchfulness, from r-q-b, to watch over. It rests on a famous hadith. A stranger in white asks the Prophet ﷺ: what is ihsan, doing it beautifully? The answer: to worship God as if you see Him; and if you don't see Him, He sees you. Sufi teachers built a sit on that line. Head a little lowered, eyes closed, watching the breath and the heart without chasing any thought. Underneath it is a verse, in Pickthall's words: “We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.” The formal sit belongs mostly to the Sufi orders, and some Muslims are wary of it. But both halves say the same thing. People forget. So you come back: with a word, or with silence.
screen: `DH-K-R — REMEMBER, AND MENTION.` · `COUNTED ON THE FINGERS.` · `MURAQABA — WATCHFULNESS.` · `AS IF YOU SEE HIM.` · then, large: `REMEMBER, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds, in two halves. First, rest your right hand open and touch your thumb to each joint of your fingers, slowly. With each touch, say a short phrase silently. If you pray, subhan Allah, or alhamdulillah. If not, one word you want to come back to: thanks, or peace. Then let your hand rest, lower your head a little, and just watch your breath, coming in and going out. When a thought swims past, see it, and let it go by. The bell holds the time.
Dhikr. Remembrance: short words of praise said again and again, and the quiet watching beside them. Seventeenth word.
Your line: remember, again. Pick one ordinary thing you do many times a day, unlocking your phone, opening a door, and let it be your cue to come back to one word, or one breath. Day seventeen.

screen: `DAY 17 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A MONTH OF NOT-EATING THAT'S REALLY A MONTH OF PAYING ATTENTION.`

18.title: a month of not-eating that's really a month of paying attention
18.hook: a month of not-eating that's really a month of paying attention
18.howItsDone: During Ramadan, adult Muslims who are able fast from dawn to sunset, eat a pre-dawn meal called suhur, break the fast at sunset with iftar, often with dates and water, and many attend extra night prayers at the mosque.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhikr, remembrance on the fingers, and the quiet watching beside it. Your line was remember, again. What was your cue, and how often did it bring you back? Day eighteen.

Look back at the last few days. Water before the prayer. The prayer itself, the body bowing. The call. The Friday gathering. Remembrance on the fingers, and the quiet watching beside it. Every one of them is a way of paying attention, a few minutes at a time. Now stretch that to a whole month. Picture a kitchen at four in the morning, lights on, a family half asleep, eating dates and eggs and drinking as much water as they can before the sky starts to pale. Then nothing, no food, not even a sip of water, until sunset. For thirty days. Today: the month that takes the whole week and makes it last.
screen: `A WEEK OF PAYING ATTENTION.` → `A KITCHEN AT FOUR IN THE MORNING.` → `THEN NOTHING UNTIL SUNSET.`

segments.voice: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. The name comes from a root, r-m-d, for scorching heat. Because the calendar follows the moon, the month slides about eleven days earlier every year, so over a lifetime it passes through every season, the long summer days and the short winter ones. The fast, sawm, is the fourth pillar. From the first light of dawn to sunset: no food, no drink. The Qur'an explains it in one line, in Pickthall's words: “Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil).” Notice what it says the fast is for. Not weight, not endurance. Taqwa, that careful awareness that wards off harm. The hunger is a tool, not the point. A hadith in Bukhari makes that sharp: whoever doesn't give up lying and acting on lies, God has no need of their giving up food and drink. An empty stomach with a sharp tongue has missed it. And the fast isn't meant to hurt anyone. The same passage excuses the sick and travelers, and scholars add the elderly, children, and women who are pregnant or nursing. Why this month? The Qur'an says it was first revealed in Ramadan. In its last ten nights is the Night of Power, and the Qur'an says: “The Night of Power is better than a thousand months.” So at sunset, when the fast breaks, often with a date and water as the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ did, people are hungry, yes. But the month has taught them to notice every sip.
screen: `RAMADAN — FROM A ROOT FOR HEAT.` · `DAWN TO SUNSET: THE FOURTH PILLAR.` · `THAT YE MAY WARD OFF EVIL.` · `THE NIGHT OF POWER.` · then, large: `THE HUNGER IS A TOOL.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Notice your body right now. Is there any hunger or thirst in it, even a little? Don't fix it. Just find where it lives: the stomach, the throat, the mouth. Then think of the next thing you'll eat or drink. Picture it, and picture receiving it slowly, like the first sip at sunset. If you pray, you can hold the word alhamdulillah ready for that moment. The bell holds the time.
Ramadan. The month of fasting, dawn to sunset, when the Qur'an was first revealed. Eighteenth word.
Your line: hunger teaches. Today, eat one meal or drink one glass of water without your phone, and notice the first bite or the first sip. Day eighteen.

screen: `DAY 18 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE PILLAR THAT'S ABOUT MONEY.`

19.title: the pillar that's about money
19.hook: the pillar that's about money; 2.5% and why
19.carry: what you give purifies what you keep
19.tomorrow: an orphan, a merchant, a man who was trusted before he was believed
19.howItsDone: Muslims whose savings are above the nisab threshold calculate zakat once a lunar year, usually 2.5 percent, and give it to people in the categories the Qur'an names, often through a mosque or charity; many time it for Ramadan.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ramadan, the month of fasting. Your line was hunger teaches. What did the first bite or sip teach you? Day nineteen.

Here's something people don't expect. Of the five pillars that hold up a Muslim life, one is a statement of faith, one is prayer, one is fasting, one is a journey. And one is about your bank balance. Not a suggestion to be nice to the poor sometimes. A number. Worked out once a year, like a tax return, with a calculator and sometimes a spreadsheet. Grandparents do it at the kitchen table with a pencil. Mosques run online calculators for it. It sounds like the least spiritual thing in the whole religion. And its name means something close to purity.
screen: `FIVE PILLARS, ONE ABOUT MONEY.` → `A NUMBER, ONCE A YEAR.` → `ITS NAME MEANS PURITY.`

segments.voice: Zakat. The root, z-k-w, holds two ideas at once: to be pure, and to grow. Think of pruning a plant. You cut some away, and what's left is cleaner, and it grows better. That's the picture. The Qur'an almost never mentions prayer without it. Again and again, in Pickthall's words: “Establish worship, pay the poor-due.” Prayer and zakat, side by side, God and neighbor in one breath. So how does it work? Once a lunar year, a Muslim whose savings stay above a set threshold, called the nisab, traditionally measured in gold or silver, gives two and a half percent of that wealth. One fortieth. Not of income, of what you've held on to for a year. Why so small? Scholars point out that it's meant to be something anyone above the line can give every single year without being ruined by it, and so it never stops. Where does it go? The Qur'an names eight kinds of people: the poor, the needy, those who collect it, people whose hearts are being won over, freeing captives, people crushed by debt, the cause of God, and the stranded traveler. And the money isn't treated as a gift from the giver. It's the poor's right, already inside your wealth, which you're handing back. Many Shia Muslims also give khums, a fifth of their yearly surplus. And beyond all of this is sadaqa, giving from the heart, any amount, anytime. A hadith in Tirmidhi counts even a smile at your brother as sadaqa. Another, in Muslim, says charity never made anyone's wealth smaller.
screen: `ZAKAT — TO PURIFY, TO GROW.` · `PRAYER AND ZAKAT, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `TWO AND A HALF PERCENT, ONCE A YEAR.` · `THE POOR'S RIGHT, HANDED BACK.` · then, large: `ESTABLISH WORSHIP, PAY THE POOR-DUE.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Think about what you have right now. Not only money. Time this week, food in the kitchen, a skill, a coat you haven't worn in two years. Let one thing come to mind that you've been holding on to longer than you need. Picture the pruning: that one thing cut away and handed on. Notice how the rest of what you have feels after it. Lighter, or heavier? Just notice. If you pray, you can offer that thing to God before you give it. The bell holds the time.
Zakat. The third pillar: two and a half percent of savings, given once a year, from a root meaning to purify and to grow. Nineteenth word.
Your line: what you give purifies what you keep. Today, give away one thing, a coin, a coat, an hour, or just a smile, and see what happens to the rest. Day nineteen.

20.title: an orphan, a merchant, a man who was trusted before he was believed
20.hook: an orphan, a merchant, a man who was trusted before he was believed
20.howItsDone: Muslims say "peace be upon him" (or write ﷺ) after the Prophet's name, never picture him, and learn his life, the sira, from the Qur'an, the hadith and the early biographies.

segments.voice: Yesterday: zakat, the pillar about money. Your line was what you give purifies what you keep. What did you give away, and how did the rest feel? Day twenty.

Think of the person you'd hand your house keys to without a second thought. Not the most impressive person you know. The most trustworthy. Maybe you couldn't even say why; they've just never once let you down. Now picture a whole city that felt that way about one man. People who argued about everything, clans who'd fight over a camel, all agreed on him. They gave him a nickname for it. And years later, many of those same people refused to believe what he told them, and still kept leaving their valuables in his care. Today: the man at the center of it all, told the way Islam tells him. In words only.
screen: `WHO GETS YOUR HOUSE KEYS?` → `A WHOLE CITY TRUSTED ONE MAN.` → `TRUSTED, NOT YET BELIEVED.`

segments.voice: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, peace be upon him. Muslims never draw or picture him; he's known through words, so words are all we'll use. He was born in Mecca, around the year 570. His father died before he was born. His mother died when he was six. His grandfather took him in, and died two years later. His uncle Abu Talib raised him after that. So when the Qur'an speaks to him later, it can say, in Pickthall's words: “Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)?” He grew up herding sheep, then traveled with the trade caravans. A wealthy widow and merchant named Khadijah hired him to lead hers, and was so struck by his honesty that she proposed marriage. By then Mecca had a name for him: al-Amin, the trustworthy. The early biographies tell a story about it. The clans were rebuilding the Ka'ba, and they nearly came to blows over who would get the honor of setting the sacred Black Stone back in its place. They agreed to let the next man through the gate decide. It was him. He spread out a cloak, set the stone on it, and had a man from each clan lift a corner, together. Then he set it in place himself. At forty, he began to receive the Qur'an. And a hadith in Bukhari tells how he stood on a hill and asked his people: if I told you an army was behind this hill, would you believe me? They said: we've never known you to lie. Then he told them his message, and many turned away. Trusted first. Believed, by many, only later.
screen: `AN ORPHAN IN MECCA.` · `A MERCHANT, AND KHADIJAH.` · `AL-AMIN — AND THE BLACK STONE.` · `WE'VE NEVER KNOWN YOU TO LIE.` · then, large: `AL-AMIN — THE TRUSTWORTHY.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Think of someone who trusts you with something. A secret, a key, a child, a password, a job. Picture them handing it over. Notice what it feels like to be trusted. Then think of one small promise you've made lately and haven't kept yet. Nothing dramatic. A call, a book to return, a message you said you'd send. Just hold it. If you pray, you can ask for help keeping it. The bell holds the time.
The Prophet, peace be upon him. An orphan, a shepherd, a merchant, called al-Amin, the trustworthy, long before most believed him. Twentieth word.
Your line: al-Amin, the trustworthy. Today, keep that one small promise you were holding. Do it quietly, before anyone reminds you. Day twenty.

21.howItsDone: Muslim children usually begin memorizing the Qur'an from the end, with the short surahs of juz' 'amma, and these are the surahs most often recited in the daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Prophet, peace be upon him, the orphan Mecca called al-Amin, the trustworthy. Did you keep that small promise? Day twenty-one.

Three weeks. Look at what's on your strand. Salaam. Bismillah. Alhamdulillah. Inshallah. The five pillars. Then al-Fatiha, verse by verse: Rabb, rahma, the Day, tawhid, the straight path, amin. Wudu, salat, the adhan. Jumu'ah. Dhikr, and the quiet watching beside it. Ramadan and zakat. The Prophet, al-Amin. Twenty words, the everyday vocabulary of a Muslim life. That's the foothills. Tomorrow the path starts climbing: the stories of the prophets, one after another. So today, at the top of the foothills, we look up at the mountain itself. The Qur'an. And we find the place where almost every Muslim starts to climb it. Oddly enough, it's at the very end.
screen: `TWENTY WORDS ON YOUR STRAND.` → `THE FOOTHILLS, DONE.` → `THE MOUNTAIN AHEAD.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an has a hundred and fourteen surahs, roughly longest first, shortest last. To make it possible to read the whole thing in a month, especially in Ramadan, it's divided into thirty equal parts. Each part is a juz'. The last one is called juz' 'amma, after its very first word. Surah seventy-eight opens, in Pickthall's words: “Whereof do they question one another?” In Arabic, 'amma yatasa'alun. So 'amma, whereof, gives the whole part its name. Juz' 'amma holds thirty-seven surahs, from seventy-eight to the end. Most are short, some only three or four lines. Many scholars place most of them among the earliest revelations in Mecca: vivid, rhythmic, full of oaths by the dawn, the night, the fig, the declining day. And this is where children begin. Not at page one, at the back. A child learns al-Fatiha, then an-Nas, the last surah, and al-Falaq, and al-Ikhlas, which you met on day ten. Then al-Kawthar, the shortest in the whole Qur'an, three verses. Then al-'Asr, and so on, backward, surah by surah. These are the ones a Muslim recites in the daily prayers, again and again, for a lifetime. Grandparents and five-year-olds know the same ones by heart. For some, the climb goes on for years, all the way up, until the whole Qur'an is held in memory; someone who does that is called a hafiz, a keeper. But almost everyone starts here, at the small end of the mountain.
screen: `THIRTY PARTS, FOR A MONTH.` · `'AMMA — WHEREOF DO THEY QUESTION?` · `THE EARLIEST, SHORTEST SURAHS.` · `CHILDREN START AT THE BACK.` · then, large: `THE SMALL END OF THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Think back over these three weeks. Let the words drift past, the greeting, the washing, the call, the fast, the one. Don't try to remember all of them. Just notice which one has stuck. Which one came back to you on an ordinary day, in the kitchen or the car, without being asked? Hold that one word. It's yours now. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for it. The bell holds the time.
Juz' 'amma. The thirtieth part of the Qur'an, the short surahs, where nearly everyone begins. Twenty-first word, and camp one is done.
Your line: the ones every Muslim child knows. Today, look up surah one hundred and three, al-'Asr, three lines, and read it once. Tomorrow, the stories begin. Day twenty-one.
